metadata.title: The mediating role of student–teacher relationships, assertiveness, and curiosity in science achievement

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 secondary microdata for 15-year-old students and applies PISA sampling weights throughout the analyses to maintain representativeness and correct for non-response and differences in sample structure. The authors also state that analyses were conducted using a multilevel model to account for student clustering within schools, which aligns with the nested sampling design of PISA. No replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is reported, so uncertainty estimation is not specified at the replicate level. Because the analysis is based on SEM with PVSCI as the outcome, the paper does not describe any ML-specific omission of weights; instead, it explicitly reports weight application for the complex survey design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is science achievement measured via PISA 2022 plausible values (PVSCI with PV1SCIE–PV10SCIE). While the paper reports PVSCI and lists the PV codes, it does not describe how missing questionnaire responses or incomplete cases were handled in the SEM estimation (e.g., whether incomplete cases were excluded or whether missingness was handled via a specific procedure). This is a reporting gap because PISA typically has non-trivial item nonresponse, and the choice of missing-data strategy can affect parameter estimates and mediation effects.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 application data for 15-year-old students (aged 15 years 3 months to 16 years 2 months) from the seventh grade onwards, including full-time/part-time students, vocational program students, and students from foreign schools within countries. The paper states that incomplete responses on science tests ranged from 1.2% to 8.5% but does not specify an explicit exclusion rule beyond the general PISA participation/completion process. Analyses were conducted with PISA sampling weights and a multilevel approach to account for student clustering within schools.

main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM path estimates: RELATST → PVSCI β=0.052 (p=0.034); Curiosity → PVSCI β=0.221 (p<0.001). Mediation (H7): RELATST → Assertiveness → Curiosity → PVSCI estimate=0.014 (p<0.001). Correlations: RELATST–PVSCI r=0.137 (p<0.01), Curiosity–PVSCI r=0.240 (p<0.01).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Science data (PVSCI; 15-year-olds), the study leveraged student–teacher relationship quality, assertiveness, and curiosity to model science achievement, finding that student–teacher relationship quality had a small but significant direct effect on PVSCI (β=0.052, p=0.034) and that curiosity showed a stronger positive association with PVSCI (β=0.221, p<0.001), with a significant sequential mediation through assertiveness and curiosity (estimate=0.014, p<0.001). This indicates that strengthening classroom relational climate and students’ socio-emotional engagement (especially curiosity) may be a practical pathway to improve science achievement, though the cross-sectional design limits causal claims.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2022 science achievement (PVSCI) for approximately 690,000 15-year-old students using a non-experimental correlational design with SEM. The model tests whether student–teacher relationship quality (RELATST) predicts science achievement directly and indirectly through assertiveness (ASSERAGR) and curiosity (CURIOAGR), with PVSCI measured via PISA plausible values (PV1SCIE–PV10SCIE). The reported results show positive associations among the constructs: RELATST correlates with PVSCI (r=0.137, p<0.01), curiosity correlates more strongly with PVSCI (r=0.240, p<0.01), and the SEM paths indicate RELATST → PVSCI β=0.052 (p=0.034) and Curiosity → PVSCI β=0.221 (p<0.001). The sequential mediation model (RELATST → Assertiveness → Curiosity → PVSCI) is significant (estimate=0.014, p<0.001). Limitations include reliance on self-report measures for socio-emotional constructs and a cross-sectional secondary-data design, so causality cannot be inferred.
